content_data.design_notes: The palette is built around a single strategic tension: authority without intimidation. The target audience has been burned before — by agencies that charged too much, by page-builder subscriptions they never finished, by promises that turned vague under pressure. They are sceptical of anything that looks expensive or slick, because expensive and slick is what previously let them down. So the background (#fafaf8) and secondary surfaces (#f5f3ef, #f0ede8) are warm off-whites — the colour of good paper, not a tech startup's white void. This warmth signals craft and steadiness rather than venture-backed hustle. It also reads as honest: no aggressive contrast tricks, no dark-mode drama. The primary text is near-black (#1a1a1a) at full weight — this is a site that does not soften its words, so the typography should not soften either. The muted text (#6b6760) is a warm grey, not a cold one, because cold greys feel corporate and this site is speaking to a sole trader or a small team owner, not a procurement committee. The accent (#2d5016) is the single most deliberate choice. It is a deep British racing green — not a startup teal, not a trustworthy bank blue. Green was chosen because it carries the implication of go, of cleared, of done — which is exactly the emotional register the guarantee needs. 'You only pay if you like it' is a statement of confidence, and deep forest green reads as grounded confidence rather than the performed enthusiasm of a bright primary colour. It is also genuinely distinctive in the web agency space, which skews heavily blue-grey, so it gives the brand a visual identity that a sceptical SME owner will not immediately associate with the agencies that previously disappointed them. The border colour (#dedad4) is warm and quiet — just enough to separate sections without imposing structure. Borders should feel like helpful organisation, not grid-obsessed design. Playfair Display for headings brings editorial weight — it is the font of a quality newspaper or a reputable firm's letterhead. This matters because the value proposition is delivered in plain language, and plain language spoken in a serif voice reads as considered rather than blunt. Inter for body text is the right counterweight: extremely legible, neutral without being cold, and familiar enough to ordinary web users that it does not distract from the words. The container max-width of 720px is a direct expression of content strategy. This is a long-form persuasion page, not a marketing brochure. Measure at 720px with 16px base keeps line length at roughly 65-75 characters — the range at which reading comprehension is highest and the eye does not fatigue. A wider container would spread the copy thin and make it feel like an afterthought. The narrow, centred column also implies that every word was chosen — which is exactly what the writing style demands.

mission_brief.text: webdesign.uk sells complete websites to small and medium UK businesses. A customer comes to us with a domain and a business, and we build them the whole site: the pages that business actually needs, the words on them, the design, and getting it live on their own domain. It is one fixed price paid once, with no ongoing fee to us and nothing the customer is locked into. They see the finished site on a private preview link and can walk away with a full refund at any point up until they accept it, at which point it becomes theirs. Changes they ask for afterwards are charged as work, and anything that is our own mistake we put right at no cost. The people buying this are business owners who need a decent website and have neither the time to make one nor the appetite for a drawn-out agency process. They are not technical. They have often been quoted far more than this by an agency, or have been sold a page builder subscription and never finished the site. They are sceptical, they have been oversold to before, and they respond to someone talking plainly about what they will actually get. The site should do three things. It should explain the offer clearly enough that someone understands it without asking. It should ask the visitor a little about themselves and what they are after, just a little, as an opening to a conversation rather than a form to be qualified by. And it should make it easy to get in touch, by email or by phone. The tone is plain, direct British English, written for someone who does not enjoy being sold to. Short sentences and ordinary words. This is a new service with no history to trade on, so it must not reach for the things a new service does not have. It should sound like a competent small studio that is confident about the work and relaxed about proving it, not like a startup announcing itself. Restraint reads as confidence here. Overselling would read as exactly the thing these buyers have been burnt by before. Avoid the whole register of agency marketing language: no talk of solutions, no bespoke digital experiences, no passion for pixels, no promises to transform anyone's business. Avoid the visual cliches of the web design trade as well, the wireframe sketches and fanned colour swatches and browser windows drawn at an angle. The site is itself the portfolio piece, so what it demonstrates matters more than what it asserts.

roadmap_brief.text: Phase one builds five pages, nothing more. The chat box and questionnaire come in a later phase, once the service behind them exists; nothing in this phase may include a chat box, an input box wired to a backend, or any form beyond a plain contact page. **index** — the home page. What webdesign.uk sells: a complete website for a small business, built and put live on the customer's own domain, for one fixed price paid once, with no ongoing fee and nothing the customer is locked into. Say what happens from first contact to going live in one short passage and point at how-it-works for the detail. State the price plainly, drawing it from the evidence base. No invented portfolio, no testimonials, no client counts, no years of experience — the site is new, and the page must not pretend otherwise; the site itself is the demonstration piece. **how-it-works** — the process from first email to live site, step by step, in plain words: what we need from the customer, what we build and show on a private preview link, the point where they accept it and it becomes theirs, that they can walk away with a full refund at any point before acceptance, that changes they ask for afterwards are charged as work, and that anything that is our own mistake is put right at no cost. **what-you-get** — exactly what is included: the pages the business actually needs, the words on them written for that business, the design, and getting it live on their own domain; and what is not included, said as plainly as what is. **faq** — the questions a sceptical buyer actually asks, answered honestly and briefly: what it costs and whether VAT applies, how long it takes, who owns the site once accepted, what happens if they walk away before accepting, what changes cost afterwards, what we need from them to start, and what happens with their domain and hosting. Every number and named commitment on this page comes from the evidence base; where the evidence base holds no answer, the page says so plainly rather than inventing one. **contact** — a plain contact page: email and phone, what to put in a first message so the reply is useful, no response-time promises, no form. Later phases, recorded here for direction only and explicitly not to be built now: the short questionnaire that asks a visitor about their business and domain as an opening to a conversation, which arrives only once the chat service behind it exists; and a portfolio section, only once there is real accepted work to show.
